subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry, Year 11
about: HSC, Matter, quantities, reactions and energy
syllabus: NSW Chemistry Stage 6 Syllabus (2017), Year 11 course, Modules 1 to 4

points.title: Pure substances and mixtures
points.brief: Elements and compounds are pure substances. Mixtures can be separated by physical means such as filtration, distillation and chromatography, based on differences in properties.

points.title: Atomic structure
points.brief: Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around it. The atomic number is the number of protons and the mass number counts protons and neutrons.

points.title: Isotopes
points.brief: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Some are radioactive. Relative atomic mass is a weighted average of the isotopes.

points.title: Electron configuration
points.brief: Electrons fill energy levels and subshells (s, p, d) in order. The outer electrons decide how an element reacts.

points.title: Periodic table trends
points.brief: Across a period, atomic radius falls and electronegativity and first ionisation energy rise. Down a group, atomic radius rises and the other two fall.

points.title: Ionic bonding
points.brief: Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain them, forming ions held in a lattice. Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when melted or dissolved.

points.title: Covalent bonding
points.brief: Non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons. Covalent molecular substances have low melting points. Covalent network solids, such as diamond, are very hard.

points.title: Metallic bonding
points.brief: Metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, which explains why metals conduct and can be bent and shaped.

points.title: Shapes and polarity of molecules
points.brief: Electron pairs push apart, giving shapes such as linear, bent and tetrahedral. Uneven sharing of electrons in an uneven shape makes a molecule polar.

points.title: Intermolecular forces
points.brief: Dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces and hydrogen bonds hold molecules to each other and explain differences in boiling points.

points.title: Allotropes
points.brief: Different forms of the same element, such as diamond, graphite and fullerenes for carbon, with different structures and properties.

points.title: Balanced equations
points.brief: Mass is conserved in a reaction, so equations are balanced with the same number of each atom on both sides.

points.title: The mole and Avogadro's number
points.brief: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles. It lets chemists count particles by weighing.

points.title: Molar mass and moles
points.brief: n = m/M, where n is moles, m is mass in grams and M is molar mass in g/mol.

points.title: Limiting reagents
points.brief: The reactant that runs out first limits how much product forms. The other is in excess.

points.title: Empirical formulas and percentage composition
points.brief: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound, found from the mass of each element.

points.title: Concentration
points.brief: c = n/V in mol/L, and other units such as g/L and parts per million.

points.title: Dilution
points.brief: Adding water lowers concentration but keeps the moles of solute, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂.

points.title: Gas laws
points.brief: Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws relate pressure, volume and temperature, with temperature always in kelvin.

points.title: The ideal gas law
points.brief: PV = nRT links pressure, volume, moles and temperature for an ideal gas.

points.title: Molar volume of gases
points.brief: One mole of any gas takes up the same volume at the same temperature and pressure, such as 24.79 L at 25°C and 100 kPa.

points.title: Synthesis, decomposition and combustion
points.brief: Synthesis joins substances, decomposition breaks one apart, and combustion burns a fuel in oxygen, giving carbon dioxide and water when complete.

points.title: Precipitation reactions
points.brief: Two solutions mix to form an insoluble solid. Solubility rules predict which ionic compounds will precipitate.

points.title: Reactions of acids
points.brief: Acids react with metals to give a salt and hydrogen, with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide, and with bases to give a salt and water.

points.title: Rates of reaction
points.brief: Collision theory explains rates. Higher temperature, concentration and surface area, and a catalyst, all speed a reaction up.

points.title: Activation energy and catalysts
points.brief: Particles must collide with enough energy to react. A catalyst gives a path with lower activation energy and is not used up.

points.title: The activity series of metals
points.brief: Metals ranked by how easily they lose electrons. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compounds.

points.title: Oxidation and reduction
points.brief: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain. They always happen together in a redox reaction.

points.title: Oxidation numbers
points.brief: Rules for assigning oxidation numbers, used to tell which species is oxidised and which is reduced.

points.title: Half-equations
points.brief: Writing the oxidation and reduction halves of a redox reaction separately, balanced for atoms and charge.

points.title: Galvanic cells
points.brief: A redox reaction split into two half-cells joined by a wire and salt bridge, so electrons flow through the wire as a current. Standard potentials predict the voltage.

points.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
points.brief: Exothermic reactions release heat, so ΔH is negative. Endothermic reactions absorb heat, so ΔH is positive.

points.title: Energy profile diagrams
points.brief: Diagrams of energy against the course of a reaction, showing reactants, products, activation energy and ΔH.

points.title: Calorimetry
points.brief: q = mcΔT measures the heat released or absorbed, such as in the combustion of a fuel or dissolving a salt.

points.title: Hess's law
points.brief: The enthalpy change of a reaction is the same however it happens, so equations and their ΔH values can be added.

points.title: Bond energies
points.brief: Breaking bonds takes energy and making them releases it. ΔH is roughly the energy to break bonds minus the energy released making them.

points.title: Entropy
points.brief: Entropy measures how spread out energy and matter are. Gases have more entropy than liquids, and liquids more than solids.

points.title: Gibbs free energy
points.brief: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG is negative.

points.title: Predicting spontaneity
points.brief: Using the signs of ΔH and ΔS to decide whether a reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures, at none, or only at high or low ones.
